keyVerseText: All they that be fat upon earth shall eat and worship: all they that go down to the dust shall bow before him: and none can keep alive his own soul.
rootMeaning: The root of דָּשֵׁן (dâshên) conveys the idea of becoming fat or growing rich, with a literal sense tied to physical fatness or prosperity. It also carries the related notions of anointing and satisfaction, suggesting a process of being enriched or made full. This root meaning goes beyond the simple English gloss of 'fat' to include the idea of flourishing vitality and blessing, as well as the ceremonial act of anointing that implies consecration and divine favor.
usageInScripture: The word דָּשֵׁן appears three times in Scripture and is consistently translated with reference to fatness or richness, whether literal or figurative. Translations such as 'all they that be fat,' 'they shall be fat,' and 'and it shall be fat' reveal a range that includes describing prosperous people, fertile land, or abundant produce. This consistent use highlights the term's association with vigor, fertility, and blessing, sometimes even personified as vigorous, stalwart individuals.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding דָּשֵׁן in its original sense enriches our grasp of biblical themes of blessing and prosperity under God's covenant. The word's connotations of fatness and vigor symbolize not only physical abundance but spiritual flourishing and divine favor. For the Christian faith, this points to the fullness of life found in Christ, who anoints and satisfies His people, making them spiritually 'fat' or rich in grace. Recognizing this word's depth invites believers to see God's provision as comprehensive, encompassing both material and spiritual vitality.
keyVerseReflection: In Psalms 22:29, the phrase 'All they that be fat upon earth shall eat and worship' uses דָּשֵׁן to depict those who are prosperous or blessed. This word emphasizes that those enriched by God will respond in worship, acknowledging His sovereignty. It highlights a divine order where true abundance leads to reverence, and even those who return to dust recognize God's lordship. Thus, דָּשֵׁן here connects material or spiritual fullness with worshipful submission to God.
